title: Otis and the Time Loop
markdown:
In a valley where the wind carried clover and wild thyme sat the peaceful town of Willow Creek, and in it lived Otis the bell-ringer. His days kept time with the grand clock tower that watched them all. Each morning unfolded the same kind way: he polished the great brass bell until it held the sun like a second day, and his kind fingers learned the path of each thick braided rope. A deep quiet joy hummed in him, an echo of the town's own pace. People cherished their days because each was much like the last: sunshine, soft breeze, the comfort of known work.

Every day, when the sun climbed high and painted the streets gold, the noon bell chimed. As the note faded, a wonderful ordinary thing happened. Folk paused and ate. They shared warm crusty bread, plump sweet berries, and sometimes Velda the rain-frog witch poured her dewdrop tea, tasting faintly of moonlight and lavender. Then, from the last chime to the gentle start of afternoon, a peculiar quiet settled. For ten minutes the town held a cozy encore of the meal's end. Soft predictability. Everyone was content.

Until one day the air felt a little different. A little tangled. Otis reached for the noon rope. A strange silvery shimmer danced in the bright light through the tower windows. He pulled. The bell did not only chime. It let out a curious bong-thrum that vibrated through sturdy stone and through Willow Creek itself. As that odd sound faded, the familiar ten minutes before lunch began to play — and this time they did not end.

The baker was just placing a warm fragrant loaf on his sill. The children were just starting tag near the fountain's gurgle. The moment lingered. Lingered. Then it happened again, exactly: loaf, tag, the same laugh about to start.

Otis felt a moth-flutter of worry against his chest. He tried the bell again, hoping to break the knot. Each pull led back to the same baker, the same children, the same ten minutes. Not a cozy encore now. A looping tangle. The town's gentle rhythm was caught. He realised, with a soft sigh, that everyone would be stuck at the very start of lunch forever: no new moment, no new story, not even a new kind of berry. He had to find the rope that had sung that strange sweet bong-thrum, before lunch, and all the precious minutes after, faded away.

He needed someone who understood whispers that hide in a misplaced drop or a soft rain. Velda's cottage nestled by the murmuring creek, always filled with damp moss and calming lavender, her croak wise and mellow as a twilight lullaby. He made his way there. The looping sounds of town grew faint and muffled as he neared. She was tending tiny shimmering frogs, her skin like polished emerald, glistening.

"Velda," Otis said, soft and a little troubled. "The noon bell has sung us into a loop."

Her large calm eyes blinked slowly, like the opening of a pond lily. She listened to his gentle explanation, webbed fingers tracing patterns on cool damp earth. She closed her eyes and let the world wash over her: rustle of leaves, trickle of creek, the distant repeated fountain, a soft wave. She hummed a low rumbling tune, warm earth after a spring shower, rain on thatch. Then she opened her eyes toward the tower, gaze distant, as if she could see through stone and metal.

"The dewdrop," she murmured, like rain on a delicate leaf. "A single misplaced dewdrop. It landed on the third rope, the one that sings the clearest note, the purest tone. It has woven a quiet enchantment of sameness."

They returned to the tower and climbed the winding stairs that spiraled higher and higher. The looping ten minutes still played below, a soft repetitive hum that made the air feel thick and slow. Otis, with Velda perched on his shoulder, her webbed feet finding a secure spot, looked at the thick strong ropes, each waiting. She pointed a delicate finger. "There."

There it was, clinging to the third rope: a tiny perfect dewdrop, catching sunlight, shimmering with an odd persistent light. So small. So unassuming. So much pause for a whole town.

With utmost care, a breath held softly, Otis reached. The air around the drop felt cool and still, as if time itself were waiting. He did not pull or tug. Force was the wrong weather for this. With a feather-light touch he nudged. The dewdrop detached as if letting go of a long-held secret and fell, a glistening pearl, silent, onto the dusty floor. As it vanished into shadow, the repeating hum faded. Natural flowing sound returned. The baker finished placing his loaf. The children's tag ran to a happy end. Then the next part of afternoon began, fresh and new. Willow Creek was free of its temporal tangle.

Relief warmed them like late sun. They shared a look that did not need a speech.

Ever since then, Otis checked the ropes for stray dew before he pulled.

The noon bell sang its usual clear note. The ten minutes felt like themselves, once each. Evening found him at his window. First stars. Lamplight on his face. The valley smelled of thyme again. He let the day fold, safe and warm, and drifted, the bell's last kind sound still somewhere in the dark.
